newsitem.title: USA: Boeing has orders for 18 business versions of 737.
newsitem.headline: Boeing has orders for 18 business versions of 737.

text.p: Orders for a new business version of Boeing Co.'s 737 jet are running far ahead of expectations less than a year after the model was launched, a company executive said.

Borge Boeskov, president of Boeing Business Jets, said in an interview that the company, a joint venture with General Electric Co., has 18 firm orders for the specially configured model of the twin-engine jet, with 15 deals signed in the first five months of this year.
Boeing expects to produce the plane, which Boeing sells for $32 million without interior fittings or paint, at a rate of 24 a year for at least the next four years, triple the initial target.
With the new version of the 737, Boeing is competing with Gulfstream Aerospace Corp. and Bombardier Inc. for a share of the growing market for executive jets.
"This market is essentially growing into the 737 family of airplanes," Boeskov said. "What we decided to do at Boeing was to attack this market and go after it."
Boeing offers an attractive proposition to corporate executives, entrepreneurs and heads of state looking for global transportation.

For about the same price as a top-of-the-line Gulfstream V or Bombardier Global Express, Boeing can offer a plane with nearly three times the space -- enough room for 12 first-class seats, sleeping quarters, a conference room and even an exercise facility.
The two smaller planes, however, can fly much higher, slightly faster and about 350 miles farther and also have the advantage of being able to take off and land at much smaller airports.
Byron Callan, an analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc., said Boeing would compete "only at the periphery" of the market for executive jets.
"Bombardier and Gulfstream specifically address the executive jet market," he said. "The main battle is going to be between those two."
So far, Boeing has sold most of its business jets to anonymous wealthy entrepreneurs, and individual sales have not been publicly announced.
That pattern was broken Monday when golfing great Greg Norman announced he had purchased one of the specially outfitted 737s for use by him and employees of his Great White Shark Enterprises Inc.
Boeskov said he expects corporate customers to represent "by far" the biggest category of buyers for the jets over time.
He said the jet also has been sold to one government for use by a head of state, and the manufacturer is in negotiations with two more governments.
The airplane, which blends components of the next-generation 737-700 and -800, will be delivered to its first customer in late 1998, with the next available delivery in late 1999.
Corprate customers typically will pay about $5 million to an outfitter to finish the plane, raising the total price tag to nearly $40 million or higher for more elaborate interior designs.
In the past, Boeing had hesitated to aggressively market its planes for corporate or private use for fear of competing with its airline customers.

But now the company believes it is not taking business away from the airlines because potential customers of private planes represent a "minuscule percentage" of business-class and first-class customers, Boeskov said.
Ultimately, Boeing would like to build versions of the jet that fly higher and faster, but Boeskov said there were no plans to develop smaller models.
